hints: Think about what you actually measure on a TLC plate with a ruler after the solvent front stops, and what you measure on a GLC trace with time.
Remember that one term is a ratio of two distances so has no units, while the other is a time interval from a clear start point to a clear end point.
walkthrough:
Picture what Rf is for**
Imagine your developed TLC plate. You see a baseline where you spotted, spots for each component part way up, and a solvent front line near the top. $R_f$ is simply asking: how far did this spot get compared to how far the solvent got. It must always be less than 1.

Write the ratio precisely**
So you measure from the baseline to the centre of the spot, and from the baseline to the solvent front, both in $\text{cm}$. Then: $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by component}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$$ It is a ratio, so it has no units.

Picture what retention time is for**
Now switch to gas liquid chromatography. There is no plate to measure. The sample is injected as a gas, carried through a long column, and each component comes out at a different time to hit the detector. The trace is signal against time.

Define the time interval**
Retention time is the time taken for that specific component to travel through the column. That is the time from injection to the peak maximum when it is detected.

Final answer: $R_f$ value = distance moved by component / spot / solute divided by distance moved by solvent front.
retention time = time between injection of sample and detection of component.

hints: Recall that in TLC the plate itself is the stationary solid, so the moving part must wash over it, while in GLC the moving part is always an inert carrier gas.
walkthrough:
Sort out which box you need to fill**
The table already crosses out TLC stationary phase and GLC mobile phase. You only need TLC mobile phase and GLC stationary phase. Think opposite in each case.

Assign the phases**
In TLC the stationary phase is the solid silica on the plate, so the mobile phase that climbs by capillarity must be a liquid solvent, it can be polar or non-polar depending on the separation. In GLC the mobile phase is an inert carrier gas such as helium, so the stationary phase coating the inside of the column must be a liquid that does not evaporate, a non-volatile high boiling point liquid.

Final answer: thin-layer chromatography mobile phase: polar or non-polar solvent / named solvent e.g. ethanol, hexane.
gas/liquid chromatography stationary phase: non-volatile / high boiling point liquid.

hints: Link larger $R_f$ to travelling further up the plate in the same time, so ask yourself whether A spent more time dissolved in the moving solvent or stuck on the solid.
walkthrough:
Translate larger Rf into movement**
A larger $R_f$ means A moved a greater distance in the same development time. It was carried further by the solvent front than B was.

Explain with competition between phases**
Separation happens because each solute keeps partitioning between being dissolved in the moving solvent and being adsorbed onto the solid silica stationary phase. If A interacts less strongly with the silica and prefers to stay in the solvent, it spends more time moving and travels further, giving the larger $R_f$.
Final answer: A is more soluble in the mobile phase / less strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase than B, so is carried further.

hints: Look for a centre of symmetry in Y, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, and in Z, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and count how many unique proton sets remain.
walkthrough:
Count environments in Y**
Draw Y as $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, hexane-2,5-dione. The molecule is symmetric through the centre of the $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ bond. The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are identical to each other, and the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups are identical to each other. That gives only 2 distinct proton environments, so 2 peaks.

Count environments in Z**
Draw Z as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, hexane-3,4-dione. It is also symmetric through the centre of the $\text{COCO}$ bond. The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups match, and the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups match. Again only 2 distinct proton environments, so 2 peaks.
Final answer: Y: 2 peaks observed; Z: 2 peaks observed.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule by counting protons on the immediately adjacent carbon atoms only, remembering that a carbonyl carbon has no protons.
For Y, check why the equivalent $\text{CH}_2$ protons next to each other do not split each other, and for Z focus on the isolated ethyl $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ unit.
walkthrough:
Remind yourself how splitting works**
Splitting follows n+1, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbons. Protons that are chemically equivalent do not split each other, they only get split by non-equivalent neighbours.

Explain Y as two singlets**
In Y, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$, the $\text{CH}_3$ is attached directly to $\text{C=O}$ which bears no protons, so n = 0, singlet. The $\text{CH}_2$ groups look like they are next to each other, but all four $\text{CH}_2$ protons are in one equivalent set because of symmetry, so they do not split each other. Their only other neighbour is $\text{C=O}$ with no protons, so they also appear as a singlet. Hence two singlets.

Explain Z as triplet plus quartet**
In Z, consider one ethyl group $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}$. The $\text{CH}_3$ sees 2 protons on the neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$, so n = 2, 2+1 = 3, triplet. The $\text{CH}_2$ sees 3 protons on the neighbouring $\text{CH}_3$, and the other neighbour is $\text{C=O}$ with no protons, so n = 3, 3+1 = 4, quartet.

Final answer: Y: two singlets.
Z: triplet and quartet.
